auditCases.family: MSHA machine guarding and hazardous energy
auditCases.observation: A miner is clearing a jammed conveyor while the belt is energized and the tail pulley guard has been removed.
auditCases.sourceReference: MSHA 30 CFR 56.14107(a), guarding of moving machine parts. MSHA 30 CFR 56.12016, locking/tagging electrically powered equipment before mechanical work.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Mine context, moving conveyor parts, removed guard, jam-clearing/mechanical work, and energized state satisfy both guarding and energy-isolation predicates.

auditCases.observation: A miner is clearing a conveyor jam after the conveyor was locked out, zero-energy verified, and access was restricted.

structuredObservation.narrative: A miner is clearing a conveyor jam.
structuredObservation.workerInteraction: No unexpected startup exposure was observed.

auditCases.sourceReference: MSHA 30 CFR 56.12016, locking/tagging electrically powered equipment before mechanical work.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: The same task terms are present, but verified lockout and no unexpected-startup exposure suppress active violation promotion.

auditCases.observation: Operator reaches near an exposed rotating shaft because the machine guard is missing while the production line is running.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.212(a)(1), machine guarding for point of operation, nip points, rotating parts, flying chips/sparks.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: General-industry machine, exposed rotating shaft, missing guard, operation, and operator exposure satisfy machine-guarding predicates.

auditCases.observation: Machine guard was removed for maintenance while the machine is locked out, zero energy verified, and the area is restricted.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147(a)(1)-(a)(2), control of hazardous energy during servicing/maintenance. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.212(a)(1), machine guarding for point of operation, nip points, rotating parts, flying chips/sparks.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Guard-removal words are disqualified by verified isolation and restricted access; only verification items remain.

auditCases.observation: Employee is using an extension cord with exposed copper conductors in a wet washdown area.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.305(g), flexible cords and cable condition/use requirements.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: In-use flexible cord, damaged insulation/exposed conductors, wet location, and employee exposure support electrical hazard and cord/wiring standards.

auditCases.family: OSHA GI electrical controlled discarded cord
auditCases.observation: Damaged extension cord is unplugged, tagged out of service, and locked in a disposal bin where employees cannot use it.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.305(g), flexible cords and cable condition/use requirements.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: The cord is damaged, but unplugged, tagged, inaccessible, and locked for disposal; active employee electrical exposure is not established.

auditCases.observation: Construction worker is framing beside an unprotected floor edge eight feet above the lower level without guardrails or fall arrest.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1), construction unprotected side/edge at 6 feet or more.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Construction, unprotected edge, lower level, and eight-foot height satisfy 1926 Subpart M edge protection predicates.

auditCases.observation: Employee could trip over a loose hose across the same-level aisle.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.22(a), walking-working surfaces kept clean, orderly, sanitary, and free of hazards.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Same-level aisle obstruction is a walking-working surface/trip issue, not an elevated-fall case.

auditCases.observation: Unlabeled spray bottle of solvent is used by multiple employees at the parts washer.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200(f), workplace container labeling and hazard communication.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Unlabeled workplace secondary container in shared use supports workplace labeling and HazCom controls.

auditCases.observation: Worker poured solvent into a small unlabeled cup for immediate use during the same shift and kept control of it.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200(f), workplace container labeling and hazard communication.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Immediate-use, under-control transfer language suppresses a final workplace-container labeling violation absent contrary facts.

auditCases.observation: At a quarry, a loader is backing through a blind area with a broken backup alarm while miners are on foot nearby.
auditCases.sourceReference: MSHA 30 CFR 56.14132(a), maintaining audible warning devices on self-propelled mobile equipment.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Mine, self-propelled mobile equipment, backing/blind-area operation, broken alarm, and miner exposure satisfy audible-warning/traffic-control predicates.

auditCases.observation: At a quarry, the loader backup alarm is broken but the loader is parked out of service with the key removed and no reverse operation.
auditCases.sourceReference: MSHA 30 CFR 56.14132(a), maintaining audible warning devices on self-propelled mobile equipment.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: A defect exists, but out-of-service/key-removed/no-reverse facts suppress active traffic exposure; repair verification remains appropriate.
Tank entry suggests possible confined-space exposure, but permit-space predicates require more facts before exact citation promotion.

auditCases.observation: Employee entered a permit-required process tank with possible toxic atmosphere, no attendant, and no pre-entry atmospheric test.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Entry, permit-space wording, atmospheric hazard, missing attendant, and missing testing satisfy permit-space control predicates.

auditCases.observation: Construction employee is working in a six-foot trench with vertical walls and no shoring, shielding, or sloping.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651 and 1926.652, excavation access, exposure, and protective systems.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Construction, employee entry, six-foot trench, vertical walls, and no protective system support excavation protective-system requirements.

auditCases.observation: A three-foot landscaping excavation is barricaded, no employee entry is occurring, and no cave-in indicators were observed.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651 and 1926.652, excavation access, exposure, and protective systems.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Depth, no entry, and barricade facts suppress protective-system citation; access/inspection questions may remain.

auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.23(b), ladder condition and use requirements. OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1053(b), construction ladder use/defect requirements.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: A vague ladder adjective does not identify defect, misuse, height, use, or jurisdiction predicates.

auditCases.observation: On a construction site, employees are using a portable ladder with a cracked side rail and loose rung.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1053(b), construction ladder use/defect requirements.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Construction, portable ladder, active use, cracked side rail, and loose rung support construction ladder defect requirements.

auditCases.observation: In a manufacturing plant, an operating conveyor has an exposed nip point and oil is leaking onto the aisle used by employees.
auditCases.sourceReference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.212(a)(1), machine guarding for point of operation, nip points, rotating parts, flying chips/sparks. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.22(a), walking-working surfaces kept clean, orderly, sanitary, and free of hazards.
auditCases.applicabilityBasis: Two independent hazards must remain separated: exposed moving parts and contaminated walking surface.
